Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
Jacobian-criterion, ample-powers, Chern-form and comparison suppliers below.
Let $X$ be a smooth projective complex scheme of pure dimension $n\ge0$.

Then the closed points of $X$ carry a structure of **complex manifold**
$X^{\mathrm{an}}$, its **analytification**: if $X\ne\varnothing$ and $n\ge1$
this is a compact Hausdorff second-countable smooth complex manifold of complex
dimension $n$
([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]); if $n=0$ it is the
finite discrete set $X(\mathbb C)$ with its unique complex structure in the
convention of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]]; and if
$X=\varnothing$ then $X^{\mathrm{an}}=\varnothing$. Every standard smooth
algebraic chart of $X$ becomes a holomorphic chart of $X^{\mathrm{an}}$, and
every morphism of smooth complex schemes $X\to Y$ induces a holomorphic map
$X^{\mathrm{an}}\to Y^{\mathrm{an}}$.

Moreover, for every ample invertible sheaf $A$ on $X$ there is a smooth
positive closed real $(1,1)$-form $\eta_A$ on $X^{\mathrm{an}}$ whose de Rham
class is the real image of the topological first Chern class
$c_1(A):=c_1(A^{\mathrm{an}})\in H^2(X^{\mathrm{an}};\mathbb Z)$:
$$J_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}[\eta_A]=\rho_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}\bigl(c_1(A)\bigr),$$
where $J$ is the de Rham comparison and $\rho$ the change of coefficients
$\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$
([[lem-rational-cohomology-scalar-comparison-for-compact-smooth-manifolds]]).
In dimension $n=0$ and for $X=\varnothing$ every $2$-form and every degree-two
cohomology class is zero and $\eta_A=0$, so the identity holds trivially.

Throughout this page, assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]): the
analytic and cohomological suppliers invoked by the results below assume full
AC, and each item records its exact use. The definitional content below uses no
choice.

**(1) Compact Kähler manifolds.** Let $n\ge1$. A **Kähler manifold** is a complex
manifold $X$ of complex dimension $n$
([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]) with complex structure
$J$ and a **Hermitian metric** $g$ — a Riemannian metric
([[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]) satisfying
$g(Jv,Jw)=g(v,w)$ for all tangent vectors $v,w$ — whose **real fundamental form**
$\omega(v,w)=g(Jv,w)$ is

- a smooth real 2-form, the section of $\Lambda^2T^*X$ obtained by alternating
  $g(J\cdot,\cdot)$;
- **positive**: $\omega(v,Jv)=g(Jv,Jv)>0$ for every nonzero tangent vector $v$;
- **closed**: $d\omega=0$.

The manifold is **compact Kähler** when the topological space $X$ is compact.

**Orientation.** For a complex basis $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of a tangent space $T_xX$,
the ordered real basis $(v_1,Jv_1,\dots,v_n,Jv_n)$ is declared **positive**. This
is well defined: two complex bases differ by a complex-linear automorphism, whose
real determinant is the square of the modulus of its complex determinant and so
is positive, and the local orientations therefore glue along holomorphic charts
to a global orientation of $X$. Let $v_1,\dots,v_n$ be a $g$-orthonormal complex
frame, so that $g(v_j,v_k)=\delta_{jk}$, and let $e_j=g(v_j,\cdot)$ and
$f_j=g(Jv_j,\cdot)$ be the metric-dual covectors. Then
$(e_1,f_1,\dots,e_n,f_n)$ is a positively oriented $g$-orthonormal coframe,
$f_j=-Je_j$ for the pullback action $(J\alpha)(v)=\alpha(Jv)$ of $J$ on
covectors, and

$$\omega=\sum_{j=1}^n e_j\wedge f_j .$$

The **oriented volume form** is the top form

$$dV:=\frac{\omega^n}{n!}=e_1\wedge f_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_n\wedge f_n ,$$

which evaluates to $1$ on each positively oriented $g$-orthonormal frame.

**Complex dimension zero.** For $n=0$ a complex manifold is a discrete space and
compactness makes it a finite set of points with its unique complex structure;
there are no tangent vectors and no forms of positive degree, $\omega=0$, and the
operators $L,\Lambda,\partial,\bar\partial,d,\partial^*,\bar\partial^*,d^*$ and
all Laplacians introduced below are zero. The Hodge star is the identity on
degree zero, and $dV$ is the counting measure.

**(2) Complex-valued forms and Kähler operators.** Let $X$ be compact Kähler.
Write $\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)$ for the complex-valued smooth $k$-forms, the
complex-linear extension of the real forms of
[[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]; the Hodge star $*$ of
[[def-riemannian-hodge-star]] extends complex-linearly, and for
$\alpha,\beta\in\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)$ the **integral inner product**

$$\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle=\int_X\alpha\wedge*\bar\beta$$

is complex-linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second; the
integral is that of
[[def-integral-of-a-compactly-supported-top-form-on-an-oriented-manifold]] and
the integrand is $\lvert\alpha\rvert^2\,dV$ when $\beta=\alpha$, so the pairing
is a positive definite Hermitian form. In holomorphic charts

$$\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}\Omega^{p,q}(X),\qquad d=\partial+\bar\partial ,$$

with $\partial$ and $\bar\partial$ of bidegree $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$
([[def-bigraded-complex-differential-forms]]); the decomposition is independent
of the holomorphic chart because holomorphic chart changes preserve bidegree.

Put $L=\omega\wedge$, so that $L:\Omega^k(X;\mathbb C)\to\Omega^{k+2}(X;\mathbb C)$,
and let $\Lambda,\partial^*,\bar\partial^*,d^*$ be the formal adjoints of
$L,\partial,\bar\partial,d$ with respect to $\langle\,,\rangle$; existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[lem-formal-adjoints-of-differential-operators-exist-and-are-unique]], applied
to the bundle of complex-valued forms with the metric of
[[prop-riemannian-metrics-induce-metrics-on-dual-tensor-and-exterior-bundles]]
and the density $dV$. The **Laplacians** are

$$\Delta_d=dd^*+d^*d,\qquad \Delta_\partial=\partial\partial^*+\partial^*\partial,\qquad \Delta_{\bar\partial}=\bar\partial\bar\partial^*+\bar\partial^*\bar\partial ,$$

and $\epsilon(k)=(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}$.

**(3) Rational pure Hodge structures.** Let $k\in\mathbb Z$. A **rational pure
Hodge structure of weight $k$** is a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-vector space
$V$ together with a direct-sum decomposition by $\mathbb C$-subspaces

$$V_{\mathbb C}=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}V^{p,q},\qquad \overline{V^{p,q}}=V^{q,p},$$

where conjugation is the $\mathbb C$-antilinear involution
$v\otimes\lambda\mapsto v\otimes\bar\lambda$. The sum is finite because
$V_{\mathbb C}$ is finite dimensional, and it is direct by definition. The **Weil
operator** $C$ is the $\mathbb C$-linear endomorphism of $V_{\mathbb C}$ acting
as $i^{p-q}$ on $V^{p,q}$; the conjugation symmetry makes $C$ commute with
conjugation, so $C$ is the complexification of a $\mathbb Q$-linear endomorphism
of $V$.

A **polarization** of such a Hodge structure is a nondegenerate $\mathbb Q$-bilinear
form $Q:V\times V\to\mathbb Q$, extended $\mathbb C$-bilinearly to $V_{\mathbb C}$,
such that

- $Q(y,x)=(-1)^kQ(x,y)$ for all $x,y$;
- $Q(V^{p,q},V^{a,b})=0$ unless $(a,b)=(q,p)$;
- $h(x,y)=Q(Cx,\bar y)$ is a positive definite Hermitian form on $V_{\mathbb C}$.

A **rational sub-Hodge structure** is a $\mathbb Q$-subspace
$U\subseteq V$ with $U_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}(U_{\mathbb C}\cap V^{p,q})$.
The **Tate shift** $V(-r)$, for $r\in\mathbb Z$, keeps the underlying $\mathbb Q$-vector
space, the Weil operator and $Q$ as they are and moves the bidegrees to
$(p+r,q+r)$, so that the weight becomes $k+2r$; equivalently, $(V(-r))^{p,q}=V^{p-r,q-r}$.

Let $X$ be a classical algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$ in the sense of
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]: a separated
quasi-compact locally ringed space over $\mathbb C$ with a finite cover by
affine models $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the morphisms being the regular maps,
i.e. the morphisms of locally ringed spaces over $\mathbb C$
([[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]]).

(a) **Analytic topology.** An affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ carries the
subspace topology of the Euclidean topology of $\mathbb C^n$
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]],
[[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). If $Z_1,Z_2\subseteq X$ are affine
models and $\varphi:Z_1\to Z_2$ is the structure-sheaf isomorphism, then on
$Z_1\cap Z_2$ the maps $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ are given locally by
polynomial quotient functions
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]) and are
therefore continuous for the Euclidean topologies: polynomial functions are
continuous, and a quotient is continuous wherever its denominator does not
vanish ([[lem-algebra-of-continuous-real-maps-on-a-space]],
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). Hence the topologies transported
from the two affine models agree on the overlap, so the affine-model topologies
glue to a unique topology on the underlying set of $X$
([[def-topological-space]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]]): the **analytic
topology** of $X$. Every regular map of complex classical varieties is
continuous for the analytic topologies, by the same local description
([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and the analytic topology refines the Zariski
topology because polynomial zero sets are Euclidean closed. Whenever a complex
algebraic variety is used as a topological space below it carries the analytic
topology, and each subvariety carries the subspace topology.

(b) **Smooth points.** Let $S$ be a classical variety over $\mathbb C$ and let
$x\in S$. The point $x$ is a **smooth point of $S$** if its algebraic local ring
$\mathcal O_{S,x}$ is a regular local ring: a nonzero Noetherian local ring
whose maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_x$ satisfies
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2)=\dim\mathcal O_{S,x}$
([[def-embedding-dimension-and-regular-local-ring]]). The residue field at a
classical complex point is $\mathbb C$. The variety $S$ is **smooth** if every
point is smooth. This intrinsic algebraic condition does not require a Zariski
neighbourhood to be algebraically isomorphic to an open subset of affine space.

(c) **Finite smooth algebraic stratifications.** A **finite smooth algebraic
stratification with the frontier condition** of $X$ is a finite decomposition
$X=\coprod_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha$ into pairwise disjoint nonempty connected
locally closed subsets $S_\alpha\subseteq X$ — the **strata** — such that each
$S_\alpha$, with its reduced induced algebraic structure, is a smooth algebraic
subvariety of $X$; and such that for every $\alpha$ the closure
$\overline{S_\alpha}$ of $S_\alpha$ in $X$ is a union of strata. The latter is
the **frontier condition**: the frontier
$\overline{S_\alpha}\setminus S_\alpha$ of every stratum is a union of strata
([[def-connected-space]], [[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]]).

**The induced structure is the polynomial-quotient function sheaf, not a
restriction of $\mathcal O_X$.** A locally closed $S\subseteq X$ is, locally
inside an affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the set of points with $h\neq0$
and $f_1=\dots=f_r=0$ for polynomials $h,f_1,\dots,f_r$ on $Z$
([[def-constructible-subset-variety]],
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]); the map
$z\mapsto(z,1/h(z))$ identifies it with the affine model
$\{(z,t):th(z)=1,\ f_1(z)=\dots=f_r(z)=0\}\subseteq\mathbb C^{n+1}$, and its
**reduced induced structure sheaf** is the one transported along this
identification: locally functions of the form $a/b$ with $b$ nonvanishing on the
set. The ambient restriction $\mathcal O_X|_S$ is not used, since already at the
origin of the affine line the ambient stalk is the local ring of the line while
the stalk of the reduced point is $\mathbb C$. An open subset of an affine model
is a union of principal open subsets, and each principal open subset is again an
affine model, so every locally closed subvariety of $X$ is a classical variety
for the induced structure sheaf. No existence theorem for stratifications, no
common-refinement theorem and no choice principle is asserted: nothing is
selected, and all cited suppliers are choice-free.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be an $R$-oriented boundaryless $n$-manifold, with $R$ commutative unital; manifolds are Hausdorff and second countable here. Then cap with the compatible compact orientation classes gives isomorphisms
$$D_M:H_c^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R)$$
for every integer $p$, including disconnected, noncompact and empty $M$.

Naturality means that for an open inclusion $i:U\hookrightarrow M$ with restricted orientation, $D_M e=i_*D_U$, where $e$ is extension of compact supports. For compact $M$, $H_c^p(M;R)=H^p(M;R)$ canonically and $D_M(a)=a\cap[M]$. For arbitrary $M$ the isomorphism is the direct sum of those on its components. AC is used in the countable coordinate-neighborhood selection for exhaustion and in the local universal-coefficient proof.

Let $M$ be a compact boundaryless $n$-manifold with a specified $R$-orientation $\mu$, where $R$ is a commutative unital ring. Its **fundamental class** is
$$[M]=[M]_M\in H_n(M,M\setminus M;R)=H_n(M;R),$$
using [[lem-compatible-local-orientation-classes-exist-over-compact-subsets]] with the compact support $K=M$. The final equality holds at the chain-complex level: $C_*(\varnothing;R)=0$, so quotienting by it leaves $C_*(M;R)$. The cited lemma proves existence and uniqueness of this class with point restriction $\mu_x$ at every $x\in M$. Thus the notation denotes a class determined by the supplied orientation, not an arbitrary generator chosen afterward.

The same lemma gives finitely many open-and-closed components $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ and the restriction isomorphism
$$H_n(M;R)\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{j=1}^k H_n(M,M\setminus M_j;R).$$
The summand on the right identifies with $H_n(M_j;R)$: apply [[thm-excision-for-singular-homology]] to remove the closed set $M\setminus M_j$, which is the entire open relative subspace. The resulting pair is $(M_j,\varnothing)$. Under this identification $[M]$ corresponds to the finite tuple of the component fundamental classes.

If the orientation is negated on one component, its new fundamental-class summand is the negative of its old one. Indeed restriction is linear, so the negative class restricts to $-\mu_x$ at all points of that component, and uniqueness in the compact-set lemma identifies it with the new class. The other component summands are unchanged. In characteristic two this negation can leave the orientation and class unchanged; no distinction between $\mu$ and $-\mu$ is imposed when they are equal.

For empty $M$ the fundamental class is $0$ in the zero homology group, with an empty direct sum. For $R=0$ the unique orientation gives the zero class. A compact zero-manifold has finitely many singleton components, and its fundamental zero-cycle has at each point the coefficient prescribed by its local module generator. The definition requires a supplied orientation and uses no AC or simultaneous choice of one orientation per component.

Fix a space $X$, abelian group $G$ and integer $n\ge0$. For a singular cocycle $\varphi\in Z^n(X;G)$ and an integral singular cycle $c\in Z_n(X;\mathbb Z)$, define their **evaluation** to be $\varphi(c)\in G$, using [[def-singular-cohomology-with-coefficients]] and [[def-singular-chain-complex-and-singular-homology]]. If $c=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma$ is its finite formal expansion, this value is $\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\varphi(\sigma)$.

The **Kronecker pairing** on quotient classes is the rule
$$\langle[\varphi],[c]\rangle=\varphi(c),\qquad H^n(X;G)\times H_n(X;\mathbb Z)\to G.$$
Its descent through both quotients, biadditivity and naturality are justified by the following lemma [[lem-the-kronecker-pairing-is-independent-of-cocycle-and-cycle-representatives]], before any use of the quotient pairing. It is not an assertion that evaluation gives an isomorphism to the full dual of homology.

For negative $n$, the two groups are zero and the pairing is the zero map. Empty $X$ and zero $G$ also give zero evaluation. When $G$ is an $R$-module, the cohomology variable is $R$-linear and the integral homology variable is additive; an $R$-bilinear pairing instead uses chains and homology over $R$ with $R$-linear cochains. No representative-selection function is included in the definition.

The Kronecker rule $\langle[\varphi],[c]\rangle=\varphi(c)$ is independent of both cocycle and cycle representatives and is additive in both variables. For a continuous $f:X\to Y$, $\alpha\in H^n(Y;G)$ and $z\in H_n(X;\mathbb Z)$, it satisfies
$$\langle f^*\alpha,z\rangle=\langle\alpha,f_*z\rangle.$$
For a coefficient homomorphism $u:G\to G'$, it satisfies $\langle u_*\alpha,z\rangle=u\langle\alpha,z\rangle$. The same representative-independence argument gives the $R$-bilinear pairing for $R$-linear cochains on chains over a commutative ring $R$.

Assume AC. For every field $k$, every space $X$, and $n\ge0$, evaluation gives a natural $k$-linear isomorphism
$$H^n(X;k)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_k(H_n(X;k),k).$$
There is no finite-dimensional hypothesis. The right side is the full algebraic dual.

A continuous map $f:X\to Y$ induces $f^*:H^n(Y;G)\to H^n(X;G)$ for every integer $n$ and abelian group $G$, by $f^*[\varphi]=[\varphi f_\#]$. These maps satisfy $(1_X)^*=1$ and $(g\circ f)^*=f^*\circ g^*$. A coefficient homomorphism $u:G\to G'$ induces $u_*:H^n(X;G)\to H^n(X;G')$, covariantly functorial in coefficients and commuting with $f^*$.

For each abelian group $G$, the assignments
$$X\mapsto C_\bullet(X;G),\qquad f\mapsto f_\#$$
and
$$X\mapsto H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G),\qquad f\mapsto H_n(f_\#)$$
define covariant functors from topological spaces to chain complexes and to
abelian groups, respectively. Equivalently,
$$\operatorname{id}_{X,\#}=\operatorname{id}_{C_\bullet(X;G)},\qquad (g\circ f)_\#=g_\#\circ f_\#,$$
and for every $n\geq 0$,
$$H_n((g\circ f)_\#)=H_n(g_\#)\circ H_n(f_\#),\qquad H_n(\operatorname{id}_{X,\#})=\operatorname{id}_{H_n(X;G)}.$$

Let $X$ be a space and $R$ a commutative unital ring. For $p,n\ge0$, $\varphi\in C^p(X;R)$, and a singular $n$-simplex $\sigma$, define
$$\varphi\cap\sigma=\begin{cases}\varphi(\sigma[0,\ldots,p])\,\sigma[p,\ldots,n],&n\ge p,\\0,&n<p.\end{cases}$$
Extend $R$-bilinearly in $\varphi$ and the finite chains of [[def-singular-simplex-and-singular-chain-group-with-coefficients]]. An $R$-linear cochain is a function on simplex generators; each value multiplies one specified back-face generator. Thus the formula is well-defined on finite formal chains and is $R$-balanced in its two inputs. It gives
$$C^p(X;R)\otimes_R C_n(X;R)\longrightarrow C_{n-p}(X;R),$$
with negative chain groups zero. This is the **cap product with cohomology first**: evaluate on the front face and retain the back face.

The face convention is the same as [[def-singular-cup-product-on-cochains]]. In terms of its Alexander–Whitney diagonal $D_X$, cap is the bidegree-$(p,n-p)$ part of $D_X$, followed by evaluation of the first factor by $\varphi$. There is no additional sign in this evaluation. Subsequent boundary and projection identities use this order.

For $p=0$, this multiplies a simplex by the value of $\varphi$ at its first vertex; in particular the constant value-one cochain acts as the identity on chains. For $p=n$, it returns $\varphi(\sigma)$ times the last vertex, a degree-zero chain, whose boundary is zero. For $p>n$ it is zero by definition. On a degenerate simplex the same face formula applies; unnormalized chains retain these generators. Empty $X$, zero inputs and the zero ring give zero maps. The construction also applies to the higher singular simplices of a point and requires no AC.

For $\varphi\in C^p(X;R)$, $c\in C_n(X;R)$, $p,n\ge0$, over a commutative unital ring,
$$\partial(\varphi\cap c)=(-1)^p\bigl(\varphi\cap\partial c-\delta\varphi\cap c\bigr).$$
Consequently cap induces an $R$-bilinear map
$$H^p(X;R)\otimes_R H_n(X;R)\longrightarrow H_{n-p}(X;R).$$
Negative chain groups are zero, and no AC is assumed.

For continuous $f:X\to Y$, $\alpha\in H^p(Y;R)$ and $x\in H_n(X;R)$,
$$f_*(f^*\alpha\cap x)=\alpha\cap f_*x.$$
For $\alpha\in H^p(X;R)$, $\beta\in H^q(X;R)$ and $x\in H_n(X;R)$,
$$(\alpha\smile\beta)\cap x=\beta\cap(\alpha\cap x).$$
Here $R$ is commutative unital and cap evaluates the front face, retaining the back face. Both identities hold already on cochains and chains. No AC is needed.

Let $X$ be a topological space and let $G$ be an abelian group. The
**augmentation at 0-simplices** is the homomorphism
$$\varepsilon_X:C_0(X;G)\to G$$
defined by
$$\varepsilon_X(\sigma\otimes g)=g$$
for every singular $0$-simplex $\sigma:\Delta^0\to X$, and extended linearly.

The **reduced singular chain complex** $\widetilde C_\bullet(X;G)$ is obtained
from the singular chain complex by replacing degree $0$ with the kernel of the
augmentation:
$$\widetilde C_n(X;G):= \begin{cases} C_n(X;G),& n\geq 1,\\ \ker\varepsilon_X,& n=0,\\ 0,& n<0. \end{cases}$$
Its differential is the singular boundary in degrees $\geq 1$ and the zero map
$\widetilde C_0(X;G)\to 0$ in degree $0$.

The **reduced singular homology groups** are
$$\widetilde H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G):=H_n(\widetilde C_\bullet(X;G)).$$
For the empty space, this convention leaves $\widetilde C_0(\varnothing;G)=0$,
so $\widetilde H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(\varnothing;G)=0$ for all $n\geq 0$.

For every topological space $X$ and every abelian group $G$,
$$\varepsilon_X\partial_1=0:C_1(X;G)\to G.$$
Consequently $\operatorname{im}\partial_1\subseteq\ker\varepsilon_X$, so the
reduced singular chain complex of
[[def-zero-simplex-augmentation-and-reduced-singular-homology]] is well
defined.

Let $X$ be a space, $R$ a commutative unital ring, $a\in H^p(X;R)$ and $b\in H^q(X;R)$, with $p,q\ge0$. Then
$$a\smile b=(-1)^{pq}b\smile a.$$
The defining cochain operation need not be graded commutative. No AC is required.

Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space, and let $G$ be an abelian group, or an $R$-module if an $R$-module structure is desired. Its **compactly supported singular cohomology** is
$$H_c^p(X;G)=\varinjlim_{K\subseteq X\text{ compact}}H^p(X,X\setminus K;G).$$
The relative groups use [[def-relative-singular-cochain-complex]]. If $K\subseteq L$, the identity map of pairs $(X,X\setminus L)\to(X,X\setminus K)$ induces the transition from the $K$ group to the $L$ group. Concretely, a cochain vanishing on all simplices outside $K$ also vanishes on all simplices outside $L$, so this transition is induced by inclusion of relative cochain complexes. The positive coboundary is the same in both, so the inclusion descends to cohomology. Identities and successive transitions compose literally on cochains.

The index is a set, being a subcollection of $\mathcal P(X)$. It contains $\varnothing$, and $K\cup L$ is compact: an open cover restricts to a cover of each of $K,L$, and the union of their two finite subcovers covers the union. As a poset, it has at most one arrow between any two objects. It therefore satisfies the three filtered-category conditions in [[def-filtered-category-and-filtered-colimit]].

Here is an explicit construction, including existence of the colimit. Represent an element by $(K,a)$ with $a\in H^p(X,X\setminus K;G)$. Declare $(K,a)\sim(L,b)$ if some compact $N\supseteq K\cup L$ makes their transition images equal. Reflexivity uses $N=K$, symmetry uses the same $N$, and transitivity uses the union of two witnessing compact sets and composition of transitions. On equivalence classes, define addition by sending both representatives to $K\cup L$ and adding there; define negation and, when applicable, scalar multiplication on representatives. If representatives are changed, pass all of the finitely many comparison witnesses to their compact union. The transitioned elements then agree, and additivity of the transition maps proves the result independent of representatives. All abelian-group or module laws hold after this passage to one common group. The class of $(\varnothing,0)$ is the zero element.

The maps $a\mapsto[(K,a)]$ form a cocone. Given any compatible family of homomorphisms from the relative groups to a group or module $T$, define the map on a class $[(K,a)]$ to be the image of $a$ under the $K$ homomorphism. Compatibility proves it constant on the displayed equivalence relation; every class has a representative, so this is the unique induced homomorphism. This is precisely the colimit universal property. In particular $[(K,a)]=0$ exactly when the image of $a$ vanishes at some larger compact support, and two representatives are equal exactly by the common-support test already given.

For compact $X$, the index $K=X$ is terminal. Sending $[(K,a)]$ to the transition image in $H^p(X,\varnothing;G)=H^p(X;G)$ is inverse to the map from this terminal group, since each representative is equivalent to its image there. Thus $H_c^p(X;G)\cong H^p(X;G)$ canonically, including the one-point and empty spaces. For $X=\varnothing$, every relative group is zero. Zero coefficients and negative degrees also give zero groups by the relative-cochain conventions.

The local compactness hypothesis gives a useful cofinal family of supports: [[thm-locally-compact-hausdorff-basics]] puts every compact $K$ inside an open $V$ with compact closure. Thus supports that are closures of relatively compact open sets suffice. The explicit common-support test proves this replacement has the same colimit: every original representative moves to such a support, and any equality witness can be enlarged to another such support. This does not require selecting a neighborhood for every compact set simultaneously. All constructions above are choice-free.

If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X A$, inclusion induces an isomorphism
$$H^n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^n(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z;G)$$
for every integer $n$ and every abelian coefficient group $G$.

Assume AC. Every smooth quasiprojective complex variety $U$ admits a smooth projective compactification $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ with reduced boundary a simple normal crossings divisor $D$. Given finitely many such compactifications, there is another dominating all of them and restricting to the identity on $U$. A morphism of smooth quasiprojective varieties extends to a morphism of such compactifications after modifying the source compactification outside its open variety.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Structure of the spaces. By [F1], $X$ and $X'$ are compact oriented boundaryless $2d$-manifolds, $U$ is an oriented boundaryless $2d$-manifold, and $j,j'$ are orientation-preserving open embeddings with dense images; $p$ is continuous with $p\circ j'=j$. The analytifications of $j,j',p$ are the maps appearing in [F1], [F2] and [F3], and $H^n(X;\mathbb Q)$, $H^n(X';\mathbb Q)$, $H^n(U;\mathbb Q)$ are the singular cohomology groups of these spaces. A nonempty Zariski-open subset of the pure $d$-dimensional variety $X'$ is analytically dense: in each of the finitely many holomorphic charts provided by [F1], the complement lies in the zero locus of nonzero polynomial functions, which has empty Euclidean interior, and the charts cover $X'$. When $d=0$ the spaces are finite discrete, the dense open embeddings are bijective, and the assertions below hold by inspection.

The morphism is the identity over $U$. We prove $p^{-1}(j'(U))=j'(U)$ as subsets of $X'$, so that $p^{-1}(j'(K))=j'(K)$ for every compact $K\subseteq U$. Let $x\in X'$ with $p(x)\in j'(U)$, say $p(x)=j(u_0)=p(j'(u_0))$ with $u_0\in U$. The set $j'(U)$ is a nonempty analytically dense subset of $X'$ and $X'$ is second countable, so countably many neighborhoods of $x$ meeting $j'(U)$ yield a sequence $u_m\in U$ with $j'(u_m)\to x$; this countable selection is supplied by AC, through the countable-choice theorem of [A1]. Continuity gives $j(u_m)=p(j'(u_m))\to p(x)=j(u_0)$; since $j$ is a homeomorphism onto the open subset $j(U)$, this means $u_m\to u_0$ in $U$; then $j'(u_m)\to j'(u_0)$ by continuity of $j'$, and uniqueness of limits in the Hausdorff space $X'$ gives $x=j'(u_0)\in j'(U)$. The reverse inclusion is immediate from $p\circ j'=j$. For compact $K\subseteq U$, every $x$ with $p(x)\in j'(K)$ lies in $j'(U)$, and on $j'(U)$ the map $p$ is $j\circ(j')^{-1}$, so $p(j'(u))=j(u)\in j'(K)$ exactly when $u\in K$.

The augmentation evaluates the Kronecker pairing through cap. For every space $M$, $\alpha\in H^n(M;\mathbb Q)$ and $z\in H_n(M;\mathbb Q)$ one has $\Phi(\alpha,z)=\varepsilon_*([\alpha\cap z])$. Choose a cocycle $\varphi$ and a cycle $z=\sum_\sigma c_\sigma\sigma$ representing the two classes; the defining cap formula in degree $n$ gives $\varphi\cap z=\sum_\sigma c_\sigma\varphi(\sigma)[\sigma(n)]$, a finite sum of last-vertex generators, and $\varepsilon_*$ of its class is $\sum_\sigma c_\sigma\varphi(\sigma)=\Phi(\alpha,z)$. Both sides are well defined on classes: cap descends by [F4] and $\varepsilon$ descends by [F5].

The pairings. For $M=X$ or $X'$ define $\Lambda_M(\alpha, eta):=\Phi(\alpha,D_M eta)$ for $\alpha\in H^n(M;\mathbb Q)$ and $ eta\in H^{2d-n}(M;\mathbb Q)$, and define $\Lambda_U(\alpha,c):=\Phi(\alpha,D_Uc)$ for $\alpha\in H^n(U;\mathbb Q)$ and $c\in H_c^{2d-n}(U;\mathbb Q)$. Each $\Lambda$ is $\mathbb Q$-bilinear and perfect: $D_M$ and $D_U$ are isomorphisms by [F2], so for $\alpha
e0$ there is $z$ with $\Phi(\alpha,z)
e0$ and $z=D eta$ for a unique $ eta$, whence $\Lambda(\alpha, eta)
e0$; conversely, if $ eta
e0$ then $D eta
e0$ and evaluation at the nonzero class $D eta$ is a nonzero functional on the full dual of homology, realized by some $\alpha$ because $\Phi$ identifies cohomology with that full dual by [F3].

Cap, cup and the fundamental class. For a closed oriented $2d$-manifold $M$, $\alpha\in H^n(M;\mathbb Q)$ and $\beta\in H^{2d-n}(M;\mathbb Q)$, one has $\Phi(\beta,D_M\alpha)=\langle\alpha\smile\beta,[M]\rangle$, where the right side abbreviates $\Phi(\alpha\smile\beta,[M])$ for the top-degree Kronecker pairing. Indeed $D_M\alpha=\alpha\cap[M]$ by [F2], and the second cap identity of [F4] gives $(\alpha\smile\beta)\cap[M]=\beta\cap(\alpha\cap[M])=\beta\cap D_M\alpha$; applying $\varepsilon_*$ and step 1.3 in degrees $2d-n$ and $2d$ gives the stated equality.

Compatibility of the pairings with the open inclusion. For $\theta\in H^n(X;\mathbb Q)$ or $\theta\in H^n(X';\mathbb Q)$ and $c\in H_c^{2d-n}(U;\mathbb Q)$, one has $\Lambda_U(j^*\theta,c)=\Lambda_X(\theta,e_Xc)$ and $\Lambda_U((j')^*\theta,c)=\Lambda_{X'}(\theta,e_{X'}c)$. Indeed $\Lambda_U(j^*\theta,c)=\Phi(j^*\theta,D_Uc)=\Phi(\theta,j_*D_Uc)=\Phi(\theta,D_X(e_Xc))=\Lambda_X(\theta,e_Xc)$ by the naturality in [F3] and the duality naturality in [F2], and the primed identity is identical.

The identity over compact supports. For every $n$ and every $c\in H_c^{2d-n}(U;\mathbb Q)$ one has $p^*(e_Xc)=e_{X'}c$ in $H_c^{2d-n}(X';\mathbb Q)$, where $p^*$ acts on the relative groups, possible by step 1.2. Choose by [F7] a compact $K\subseteq U$ and $c_K\in H^{2d-n}(U,U\setminus K;\mathbb Q)$ representing $c$; the extension maps send $c$ to the colimit classes represented by $(j^*)^{-1}c_K$ and $((j')^*)^{-1}c_K$. By step 1.2, $p^{-1}(K)=K$, so $p$ induces a map of pairs $(X',X'\setminus K)\to(X,X\setminus K)$ and $p^*$ is defined on these relative groups. Functoriality of pullback gives $(j')^*\circ p^*=(p\circ j')^*=j^*$, so $(j')^*(p^*((j^*)^{-1}c_K))=j^*(j^*)^{-1}c_K=c_K=(j')^*((j')^*)^{-1}c_K$, and injectivity of the excision isomorphism $(j')^*$ gives $p^*((j^*)^{-1}c_K)=((j')^*)^{-1}c_K$; the two colimit classes therefore coincide.

The transfer and its adjointness. For each $n$ let $T_n:=D_X^{-1}\circ p_*\circ D_{X'}:H^n(X';\mathbb Q)\to H^n(X;\mathbb Q)$, a composite of the duality isomorphisms and the pushforward of [F2] and [F3]. Then, for all $a\in H^n(X';\mathbb Q)$ and $b\in H^{2d-n}(X;\mathbb Q)$, one has $\Lambda_X(T_na,b)=\Lambda_{X'}(a,p^*b)$. Write $\sigma=n(2d-n)$. Using step 2.1 and the definition of $T_n$, $\Lambda_X(T_na,b)=\Phi(T_na,D_Xb)=\langle b\smile T_na,[X]\rangle=(-1)^\sigma\langle T_na\smile b,[X]\rangle=(-1)^\sigma\Phi(b,D_XT_na)=(-1)^\sigma\Phi(b,p_*D_{X'}a)$, where the third equality is [F6] and the last is the defining property $D_X\circ T_n=p_*\circ D_{X'}$; naturality from [F3] turns the last term into $(-1)^\sigma\Phi(p^*b,D_{X'}a)$. On the other side, $\Lambda_{X'}(a,p^*b)=\Phi(a,D_{X'}p^*b)=\langle p^*b\smile a,[X']\rangle=(-1)^\sigma\langle a\smile p^*b,[X']\rangle=(-1)^\sigma\Phi(p^*b,D_{X'}a)$ by step 2.1 and [F6]. The two displayed values agree.

The identity on $U$. For every $a\in H^n(X';\mathbb Q)$ one has $j^*(T_na)=(j')^*(a)$ in $H^n(U;\mathbb Q)$. By perfectness of $\Lambda_U$ in its first variable (step 1.4), it suffices to test against every $c\in H_c^{2d-n}(U;\mathbb Q)$: $\Lambda_U(j^*(T_na),c)=\Lambda_X(T_na,e_Xc)=\Lambda_{X'}(a,p^*(e_Xc))=\Lambda_{X'}(a,e_{X'}c)=\Lambda_U((j')^*a,c)$, where the first and last equalities are step 2.2, the second is step 3.1 and the third is step 2.3.

Equality of the images. Let $b\in H^n(X;\mathbb Q)$. Then $(j')^*(p^*b)=(p\circ j')^*b=j^*b$, by functoriality of pullback [F1, F3], so the image of $H^n(X;\mathbb Q)$ in $H^n(U;\mathbb Q)$ is contained in the image of $H^n(X';\mathbb Q)$. Conversely, if $a\in H^n(X';\mathbb Q)$, step 4.1 exhibits $(j')^*a=j^*(T_na)$ with $T_na\in H^n(X;\mathbb Q)$, so the reverse inclusion holds and the two images agree for every $n$ with $0\le n\le 2d$. For $n<0$ or $n>2d$ both cohomology groups vanish by duality [F2] and the vanishing conventions of [F3], so both images are $\{0\}$; if $U=\varnothing$ then $X=X'=\varnothing$ because $U$ has dense image, and all groups vanish. This proves the first sentence of the statement.

Independence of arbitrary smooth projective compactifications. Let $X$ be an arbitrary smooth projective compactification of $U$, with no SNC hypothesis on its boundary, and let $Z$ be one with reduced SNC boundary, which exists by the first clause of [F8]. Apply the extension clause of [F8] to the identity morphism $U\to U$, viewed with source compactification $Z$ and target compactification $X$: by the closing remark of [F8] the clause is available for arbitrary smooth projective compactifications of the open variety, and it yields a smooth projective compactification $Y$ of $U$ with reduced SNC boundary together with morphisms $Y\to Z$ and $Y\to X$ restricting to the identity on $U$. Since $Y$ is projective and $X$ and $Z$ are separated, the morphisms $Y\to X$ and $Y\to Z$ are proper by [[lem-proper-source-to-separated-target-proper]], so step 5.1 applies to each and gives, for every $n$, $\operatorname{im}(H^n(X;\mathbb Q)\to H^n(U;\mathbb Q))=\operatorname{im}(H^n(Y;\mathbb Q)\to H^n(U;\mathbb Q))=\operatorname{im}(H^n(Z;\mathbb Q)\to H^n(U;\mathbb Q))$. Hence the image subgroup attached to a smooth projective compactification of $U$ is independent of the compactification and may always be computed from one with SNC boundary: any identity expressing that subgroup for an SNC compactification, in particular the compactification-image formula of logarithmic weights, holds for every smooth projective compactification. This proves the second sentence of the statement.

Choice accounting and boundary cases. AC is assumed in the statement and is consumed exactly through the suppliers of [F1]--[F8]: the analytification with its Chern-form, Jacobian-criterion, ample-power and comparison inputs, Poincare duality with its orientation classes and exhaustions, the full-dual universal coefficient statement, the compact-support colimit and excision, the resolution, principalization and Serre-generation inputs of [F8], and the single countable selection of step 1.2; all cap, cup, pairing and sequence computations are choice-free. Boundary cases: for $d=0$ all spaces are finite discrete, the groups vanish above degree $0$, $H^0$ has dimension the number of points, $p$ is bijective over $U$ and both images agree; for $U=\varnothing$ all groups vanish; for $n$ outside $0,\ldots,2d$ both groups vanish; for an isomorphism $p$ the transfer $T_n$ is the identity; disconnected $X,X',U$ are covered because [F2] and [F3] decompose along components and all formulas are componentwise; the compact support $K$ of step 2.3 may be enlarged and the class $c=0$ or empty $K$ give zero in the same way. Properness of $p$ is stated but not used beyond continuity and $p\circ j'=j$, both of which hold for any morphism of compactifications; no Hodge theory, strictness or mixed structure is used, and no identification of infinite-dimensional vector spaces with double duals is made.

boundaries.evidence: If $U=\varnothing$ then $X=X'=\varnothing$ because $U$ has dense image, and all groups vanish, as recorded in step 5.1.
The zero class and empty support: $c=0$ or $K=\varnothing$ give the zero compactly supported class, and both sides of the transfer identity vanish, as noted in step 7.1.
Degree zero and dimension zero: $d=0$ makes the spaces finite discrete (step 1.1), and $n=0$ is an endpoint handled in step 5.1.
Degenerate modifications: if $p$ is an isomorphism or $X=X'$, the transfer $T_n$ is the identity and the two images coincide trivially, as noted in step 7.1.
The endpoint degrees $n=0$ and $n=2d$ and the disconnected case are covered in steps 5.1 and 7.1, where the pairings decompose componentwise.
AC is consumed only through the duality and universal-coefficient suppliers and the countable selection of step 1.2, recorded in [A1] and in step 7.1.

No converse is asserted; the reverse inclusion is the content of step 4.1 and is proved there.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
Jacobian-criterion, ample-powers, Chern-form and comparison suppliers below.
Let $X$ be a smooth projective complex scheme of pure dimension $n\ge0$.

Then the closed points of $X$ carry a structure of **complex manifold**
$X^{\mathrm{an}}$, its **analytification**: if $X\ne\varnothing$ and $n\ge1$
this is a compact Hausdorff second-countable smooth complex manifold of complex
dimension $n$
([[def-complex-manifolds-and-holomorphic-vector-bundles]]); if $n=0$ it is the
finite discrete set $X(\mathbb C)$ with its unique complex structure in the
convention of
[[def-compact-kahler-manifold-and-hodge-polarization-conventions]]; and if
$X=\varnothing$ then $X^{\mathrm{an}}=\varnothing$. Every standard smooth
algebraic chart of $X$ becomes a holomorphic chart of $X^{\mathrm{an}}$, and
every morphism of smooth complex schemes $X\to Y$ induces a holomorphic map
$X^{\mathrm{an}}\to Y^{\mathrm{an}}$.

Moreover, for every ample invertible sheaf $A$ on $X$ there is a smooth
positive closed real $(1,1)$-form $\eta_A$ on $X^{\mathrm{an}}$ whose de Rham
class is the real image of the topological first Chern class
$c_1(A):=c_1(A^{\mathrm{an}})\in H^2(X^{\mathrm{an}};\mathbb Z)$:
$$J_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}[\eta_A]=\rho_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}\bigl(c_1(A)\bigr),$$
where $J$ is the de Rham comparison and $\rho$ the change of coefficients
$\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$
([[lem-rational-cohomology-scalar-comparison-for-compact-smooth-manifolds]]).
In dimension $n=0$ and for $X=\varnothing$ every $2$-form and every degree-two
cohomology class is zero and $\eta_A=0$, so the identity holds trivially.

Let $X$ be a classical algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$ in the sense of
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]: a separated
quasi-compact locally ringed space over $\mathbb C$ with a finite cover by
affine models $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the morphisms being the regular maps,
i.e. the morphisms of locally ringed spaces over $\mathbb C$
([[def-morphism-locally-ringed-spaces]]).

(a) **Analytic topology.** An affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ carries the
subspace topology of the Euclidean topology of $\mathbb C^n$
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[rem-complex-euclidean-space-dictionary]],
[[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). If $Z_1,Z_2\subseteq X$ are affine
models and $\varphi:Z_1\to Z_2$ is the structure-sheaf isomorphism, then on
$Z_1\cap Z_2$ the maps $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{-1}$ are given locally by
polynomial quotient functions
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]) and are
therefore continuous for the Euclidean topologies: polynomial functions are
continuous, and a quotient is continuous wherever its denominator does not
vanish ([[lem-algebra-of-continuous-real-maps-on-a-space]],
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). Hence the topologies transported
from the two affine models agree on the overlap, so the affine-model topologies
glue to a unique topology on the underlying set of $X$
([[def-topological-space]], [[def-subspace-topology-top]]): the **analytic
topology** of $X$. Every regular map of complex classical varieties is
continuous for the analytic topologies, by the same local description
([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and the analytic topology refines the Zariski
topology because polynomial zero sets are Euclidean closed. Whenever a complex
algebraic variety is used as a topological space below it carries the analytic
topology, and each subvariety carries the subspace topology.

(b) **Smooth points.** Let $S$ be a classical variety over $\mathbb C$ and let
$x\in S$. The point $x$ is a **smooth point of $S$** if its algebraic local ring
$\mathcal O_{S,x}$ is a regular local ring: a nonzero Noetherian local ring
whose maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_x$ satisfies
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2)=\dim\mathcal O_{S,x}$
([[def-embedding-dimension-and-regular-local-ring]]). The residue field at a
classical complex point is $\mathbb C$. The variety $S$ is **smooth** if every
point is smooth. This intrinsic algebraic condition does not require a Zariski
neighbourhood to be algebraically isomorphic to an open subset of affine space.

(c) **Finite smooth algebraic stratifications.** A **finite smooth algebraic
stratification with the frontier condition** of $X$ is a finite decomposition
$X=\coprod_{\alpha\in A}S_\alpha$ into pairwise disjoint nonempty connected
locally closed subsets $S_\alpha\subseteq X$ — the **strata** — such that each
$S_\alpha$, with its reduced induced algebraic structure, is a smooth algebraic
subvariety of $X$; and such that for every $\alpha$ the closure
$\overline{S_\alpha}$ of $S_\alpha$ in $X$ is a union of strata. The latter is
the **frontier condition**: the frontier
$\overline{S_\alpha}\setminus S_\alpha$ of every stratum is a union of strata
([[def-connected-space]], [[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]]).

**The induced structure is the polynomial-quotient function sheaf, not a
restriction of $\mathcal O_X$.** A locally closed $S\subseteq X$ is, locally
inside an affine model $Z\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, the set of points with $h\neq0$
and $f_1=\dots=f_r=0$ for polynomials $h,f_1,\dots,f_r$ on $Z$
([[def-constructible-subset-variety]],
[[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]); the map
$z\mapsto(z,1/h(z))$ identifies it with the affine model
$\{(z,t):th(z)=1,\ f_1(z)=\dots=f_r(z)=0\}\subseteq\mathbb C^{n+1}$, and its
**reduced induced structure sheaf** is the one transported along this

$F^pV=F^{p+1}V+(F^pV\cap\bar F^{n-p}V)$, and the vanishing condition makes
this sum direct; descending induction through the finite filtration gives
$F^pV=\bigoplus_{a\ge p}(F^aV\cap\bar F^{n-a}V)$ and then the decomposition
of $V$. Conversely, the decomposition gives these two conditions by grouping
its summands by the first and second indices.

**Morphisms.** A morphism $f\colon H\to K$ of rational mixed Hodge structures
is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear map with $f(W_aH)\subseteq W_aK$ for all $a$ and
$f_{\mathbb C}(F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq F^pK_{\mathbb C}$ for all $p$, where
$f_{\mathbb C}=f\otimes\mathrm{id}$. Such an $f$ commutes with the
conjugations $\sigma$, hence also satisfies
$f_{\mathbb C}(\bar F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq\bar F^pK_{\mathbb C}$.

**Substructures, pure structures, Tate.** A subspace $H'\subseteq H$ with the
induced filtrations $W_aH'=H'\cap W_aH$ and
$F^pH'_{\mathbb C}=H'_{\mathbb C}\cap F^pH_{\mathbb C}$ is a **substructure**
when the induced filtrations again satisfy the opposition condition on every
graded piece, and a quotient $H\to Q$ with the quotient filtrations is a
**quotient structure** under the same requirement; that the kernel, image and
cokernel of a morphism do carry such structures is not part of the definition
and is proved in the strictness lemma below. A structure is **pure of weight
$n$** when $W_{n-1}H=0$ and $W_nH=H$; the opposition condition then says that
$H_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}$ with
$H^{p,q}=F^p\cap\bar F^q$, and $\overline{H^{p,q}}=H^{q,p}$. The **Tate
structure** $\mathbb Q(r)$, for $r\in\mathbb Z$, is the pure structure of
weight $-2r$ with $\mathbb Q(r)_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C$ concentrated in type
$(-r,-r)$, that is $H^{-r,-r}=\mathbb C$ and $H^{p,q}=0$ for
$(p,q)\ne(-r,-r)$.

**Tensor and dual conventions.** The tensor product $H\otimes K$ carries
$$W_a(H\otimes K)=\sum_{b+c=a}W_bH\otimes W_cK,\qquad F^p(H\otimes K)_{\mathbb C}=\sum_{b+c=p}F^bH_{\mathbb C}\otimes F^cK_{\mathbb C},$$
where the sums of subspaces are those of the complexifications, and the dual
$H^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(H,\mathbb Q)$ carries
$$W_aH^*=\{u:u(W_{-a-1}H)=0\},\qquad F^pH^*_{\mathbb C}=\{u:u(F^{1-p}H_{\mathbb C})=0\}.$$

**Polarizability.** A pure rational Hodge structure $H$ of weight $n$ is
**polarizable** when it carries a rational bilinear form $Q$ of parity
$(-1)^n$ that pairs only complementary Hodge types, i.e.
$Q(H^{p,q},H^{p',q'})=0$ unless $p'=n-p$ and $q'=n-q$, and whose
Weil-operator Hermitian form $h(u,v):=Q(Cu,\bar v)$, where the Weil operator
$C$ acts as $i^{p-q}$ on $H^{p,q}$, is positive definite.

No mixed structure in this definition is assumed to split over $\mathbb R$ or
over $\mathbb Q$; the Deligne splitting constructed below is a decomposition
over $\mathbb C$ only.

A **rational cohomological mixed Hodge complex** consists of

(a) a bounded-below cochain complex $K_{\mathbb Q}$ of $\mathbb Q$-vector
spaces with an increasing filtration $W$ by subcomplexes, finite on each
cochain group;

(b) a cochain complex $K_{\mathbb C}$ of $\mathbb C$-vector spaces with an
increasing filtration $W$ by subcomplexes and a decreasing filtration $F$ by
subcomplexes, again finite on each cochain group;

(c) a morphism of complexes
$\alpha\colon K_{\mathbb Q}\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C\to K_{\mathbb C}$
compatible with the weight filtrations, such that for every $w$ the induced map
$\operatorname{Gr}^W_w\alpha$ is a quasi-isomorphism,

subject to the following axiom: for every integer $w$ the weight-graded
complex $\operatorname{Gr}^W_wK$ has finite-dimensional cohomology, its
differential (induced by $d_K$) is strict for the induced filtration $F$, and
for every $r$ the induced filtration $F$ on
$H^r(\operatorname{Gr}^W_wK_{\mathbb C})$, together with the induced rational
comparison
$H^r(\operatorname{Gr}^W_wK_{\mathbb Q})\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C\to
H^r(\operatorname{Gr}^W_wK_{\mathbb C})$, is a pure Hodge structure of weight
$r+w$ ([[def-rational-mixed-hodge-structure]]).

Here a cochain complex is a complex in the sense of
[[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]], a filtration by subcomplexes is
a filtered complex in the sense of [[def-filtered-chain-complex]], a morphism
compatible with the weight filtrations is a filtered chain map in the sense of
[[def-filtered-chain-map]], quasi-isomorphism means
[[def-quasi-isomorphism]], and finiteness on a cochain group $K^n$ means
$W_aK^n=0$ for all sufficiently negative $a$ and $W_aK^n=K^n$ for all
sufficiently positive $a$, with bounds depending on $n$; dually $F^pK^n=K^n$
for $p\ll0$ and $F^pK^n=0$ for $p\gg0$.

**The weight filtration on cohomology** is the shifted image filtration
$$W_mH^n(K):=\operatorname{im}\bigl(H^n(W_{m-n}K)\to H^n(K)\bigr).$$
The shift is essential: it is what makes the axiom's weight $r+w$ on the graded
complexes compatible with the weight of $H^n$, and pole-count weight on a
logarithmic complex is not the weight on its cohomology. The differential
strictness in the axiom is Deligne's condition (GH1); the equivalent
formulation that the $F$-spectral sequence of the graded complex degenerates at
its first page is recorded in the sources but is neither asserted nor used
here, so no degeneration theorem enters this definition.

**Morphisms and the sheaf case.** A morphism of cohomological mixed Hodge
complexes is a pair of chain maps $K_{\mathbb Q}\to L_{\mathbb Q}$ and
$K_{\mathbb C}\to L_{\mathbb C}$ compatible with both filtrations and with the
comparisons; compatible filtered homotopies are permitted. The same
definitions apply to bounded-below complexes of sheaves on a topological space
when the complexes are replaced by their derived global sections and the
resolutions used preserve the graded pieces; the existence of such resolutions
for the concrete complexes used later is proved where those complexes are
constructed, not here.

(i) Let $K$ be a rational cohomological mixed Hodge complex
([[def-cohomological-mixed-hodge-complex]]). Then for every $n$ the vector
space $H^n(K_{\mathbb Q})$ carries a mixed Hodge structure whose weight
filtration is the shifted image filtration
$W_mH^n(K)=\operatorname{im}(H^n(W_{m-n}K)\to H^n(K))$ and whose Hodge
filtration is the image filtration
$F^pH^n(K_{\mathbb C})=\operatorname{im}(H^n(F^pK_{\mathbb C})\to H^n(K_{\mathbb C}))$.
In the weight spectral sequence $E_1^{p,q}=H^{p+q}(\operatorname{Gr}^W_{-p}K)$
one has $E_1^{p,q}$ pure of weight $q$, the sequence degenerates at $E_2$, and
$\operatorname{Gr}^W_mH^n(K)\cong E_2^{n-m,m}$ compatibly with the Hodge
filtrations. A morphism of cohomological mixed Hodge complexes induces, on
every $H^n$, a morphism of the resulting mixed Hodge structures.

(ii) Let $K^\bullet$ be a cosimplicial system of weight-zero rational Hodge
complexes concentrated in nonnegative cohomological degrees: cochain complexes
$K^{p,q}$ with coface maps and an internal differential satisfying the
cosimplicial identities, with $K^{p,q}=0$ unless $p,q\ge0$, whose differentials
are strict for the Hodge filtration, and with $H^q(K^p)$, together with the
induced $F$ and the rational comparison, a pure Hodge structure of weight $q$
for all $p,q$ (the axioms (GH1)-(GH2) of a cohomological Hodge complex of
weight zero). Form its simple
complex $sK$ with the standard total differential and the increasing filtration
$L$ by cosimplicial degree, $L_{-p}sK^n=\bigoplus_{i\ge p}K^{i,n-i}$. Then $sK$
is a rational cohomological mixed Hodge complex for the filtration $L$ and the
Hodge filtrations of the $K^p$, the cosimplicial spectral sequence
$E_1^{p,q}=H^q(K^p)\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(sK)$ degenerates at $E_2$, and
$\operatorname{Gr}^W_qH^n(sK)\cong E_2^{n-q,q}$; consequently all weights of
$H^n(sK)$ are at most $n$.

Every morphism $f\colon H\to K$ of rational mixed Hodge structures is strict for
$W$ and for $F$:
$$f(W_nH)=f(H)\cap W_nK,\qquad f(F^pH_{\mathbb C})=f(H_{\mathbb C})\cap F^pK_{\mathbb C}$$
for all $n,p$. Its kernel, image and cokernel, with the induced or quotient
filtrations, are mixed Hodge structures; the functor $\operatorname{Gr}^W_n$ is
exact; and a morphism from a structure of weights at least $n$ (that is
$W_{n-1}H=0$) to a structure of weights at most $n$ (that is $W_nK=K$) has
pure image of weight $n$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a topological space $X$, let
$$\Gamma(X,-):\mathrm{Ab}(X)\to\mathbf{Ab}$$
be the additive left exact global-sections functor
([[def-global-sections-functor-sheaves]]), and let $I$ be the supplied
functorial injective resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ of
[[thm-abelian-sheaves-have-enough-injectives]]: it assigns to every abelian
sheaf $\mathcal F$ one specific injective resolution
$0\to\mathcal F\to I^\bullet(\mathcal F)$
([[def-right-derived-object-relative-to-injective-resolution-data]]).

For every $q\ge0$ and every abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $X$ define the
**$q$-th sheaf cohomology group of $\mathcal F$** to be the right derived
object of $\Gamma(X,-)$ relative to $I$:
$$H^q(X,\mathcal F):=R_I^q\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)=H^q\bigl(\Gamma(X,I^\bullet(\mathcal F)_{\mathrm{del}})\bigr),$$
the cohomology object of the complex
$\Gamma(X,I^0(\mathcal F))\to\Gamma(X,I^1(\mathcal F))\to\cdots$ of abelian
groups obtained from the deleted resolution
([[def-deleted-resolution]], [[def-cohomology-object-of-a-cochain-complex]]).
We also set $H^q(X,\mathcal F):=0$ for $q<0$.

Because $I$ is a fixed supplied datum, the group $H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ is a
specific group for each pair $(X,\mathcal F)$, and for a morphism
$\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of abelian sheaves we write
$H^q(X,\varphi):=R_I^q\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ for the induced map; it is the map on
cohomology induced by $\Gamma(X,-)$ applied to the cochain maps supplied with
the datum, and it is additive in $\varphi$.

If $J$ is another supplied injective resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ then
$R_I^q\Gamma(X,-)$ and $R_J^q\Gamma(X,-)$ are naturally isomorphic, so the
$H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ computed from $J$ agree with the ones above up to a
canonical natural isomorphism; the Axiom of Dependent Choice needed for that
comparison follows from AC
([[thm-right-derived-functors-from-two-supplied-injective-resolution-data-are-naturally-isomorphic]],
[[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]). The notation
$H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ therefore does not depend on the datum used, up to this
canonical isomorphism, and we call $q$ the **cohomological degree**.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, and let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space. Then
the abelian category $\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$ of $\mathcal O_X$-modules has
enough injectives: every $\mathcal O_X$-module embeds into an injective
$\mathcal O_X$-module, and the functorial injective embedding supplied by the
Grothendieck injective-embedding theorem for Grothendieck categories supplies,
by iteration of cokernels, one specific injective resolution
$$0\to\mathcal F\to I^0(\mathcal F)\to I^1(\mathcal F)\to\cdots$$
to each $\mathcal O_X$-module $\mathcal F$ with no further selection
([[def-injective-resolution-in-an-abelian-category]]). The Axiom of Choice
enters exactly through that embedding theorem applied to
$\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$; the category-theoretic verification below is
choice-free.

Let $X$ be a separated finite-type complex algebraic variety, i.e. a classical
algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]), regarded as
a topological space with its analytic topology
([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]), and
let $k$ be a field. Write $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ for the category of sheaves
of $k$-vector spaces and $k$-linear morphisms
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]],
[[def-presheaf-of-groups-rings-modules]], [[def-module-on-ringed-space]]); it is
an abelian category ([[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]]), so its
bounded derived category $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is defined with the
conventions of [[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]], under the
standing smallness hypothesis recorded there.

The category $D_c^b(X;k)$ is the full subcategory of
$D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ consisting of the complexes $A$ satisfying:

1. $A$ is **cohomologically bounded**: $H^j(A)=0$ for $|j|$ sufficiently large;
   and
2. $A$ is **algebraically constructible**: there exists a finite smooth
   algebraic stratification with the frontier condition $\mathfrak S$ of $X$
   ([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]) such
   that for every stratum $S\in\mathfrak S$ and every integer $j$ the
   restriction $H^j(A)|_S$ is locally constant of finite rank
   ([[def-locally-constant-sheaf-of-finite-rank]]).

These are topological constructible sheaves, not coherent or quasi-coherent
sheaves. We use the shift convention of
[[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]]: $H^j(A[m])=H^{j+m}(A)$. A
groupoid local system is identified with a locally constant sheaf only through
an explicit local comparison, which is not made here.

Constructibility is a condition on the cohomology sheaves of a complex, and it
is quantified existentially over finite smooth algebraic frontier
stratifications: no stratification is fixed, and no existence or
common-refinement theorem for stratifications is asserted by this definition.
Shifting replaces $H^j$ by $H^{j+m}$, which preserves cohomological boundedness
and shifts a witnessing stratification nowhere, so the class is closed under
shifts and under isomorphisms in $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$. No choice
principle is used.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a metric space
([[def-metric-space]]) having a neighbourhood basis of contractible open sets at
every point, and let $k$ be a field. Write $k_X$ for its constant sheaf. There
are natural isomorphisms
$$H^q(X,k_X)\cong H^q_{\operatorname{sing}}(X;k)$$
in every degree, where the left side is derived cohomology in the category of
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces (computed with the functorial $k$-linear injective
resolutions supplied by
[[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]; compare
[[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]). The same assertion holds on
every open subset of $X$. In particular a nonempty contractible space with this
local property has constant-sheaf cohomology $k$ in degree zero and zero
otherwise. This applies to every finite-polyhedral open star and to its
nonempty intersection with a closed simplex.

Assume AC. Every smooth quasiprojective complex variety $U$ admits a smooth projective compactification $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ with reduced boundary a simple normal crossings divisor $D$. Given finitely many such compactifications, there is another dominating all of them and restricting to the identity on $U$. A morphism of smooth quasiprojective varieties extends to a morphism of such compactifications after modifying the source compactification outside its open variety.

Assume AC. Let $p:X'\to X$ be a proper morphism between smooth projective complex varieties of equal pure dimension, restricting to the identity on a common open variety $U$. Then $H^n(X,\mathbb Q)$ and $H^n(X',\mathbb Q)$ have the same image in $H^n(U,\mathbb Q)$ for every $n$. Consequently the compactification-image formula of logarithmic weights extends from an SNC compactification to every smooth projective compactification.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

(Actual filtered global-section models and a single comparison.) The sheaf comparison in step 3.1 is a zigzag, so it must not be treated as a nonexistent direct sheaf map in the opposite direction. (Strictness on the weight-graded global models.) This implies strictness of the differential of this actual filtered vector-space complex: if $dx$ belongs to $F^p$, take the leading $F$ index $b<p$ of $x$; its class in the associated-graded complex is a cycle. Degeneration means this $E_1$ class lifts to an actual cycle $y\in F^b$, up to an element of $F^{b+1}$ and a boundary in $F^b$. Subtract that cycle and boundary from $x$, preserving $dx$ and raising the filtration index of the preimage. Repeat through the finite filtration until a preimage of $dx$ lies in $F^p$. Thus $\operatorname{im}d\cap F^p=d(F^p)$. Moreover its degree-$r$ cohomology is $H^{r-a}(D^{[a]};\mathbb Q)(-a)$ under the comparison of step 3.1, with the induced $F$, pure of weight $r-a+2a=r+a$ and finite-dimensional by [F3]. (The mixed structure and its spectral sequence.) Apply the full conclusion of [F5] to the proved mixed Hodge complex of step 5.1. Its cohomology is $H^n(U;\mathbb Q)$ by steps 3.1-5.1 and [F6], and it carries the image Hodge filtration and shifted weight filtration $W_mH^n(U)=\operatorname{im}(H^n(W_{m-n}K)\to H^n(K))$. Also $W_nH^n(U)$ is the image of $H^n(W_0K)$. Assume AC. For every field $k$, every space $X$, and $n\ge0$, evaluation gives a natural $k$-linear isomorphism
$$H^n(X;k)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_k(H_n(X;k),k).$$
There is no finite-dimensional hypothesis. The right side is the full algebraic dual.

Assume AC. Let $U$ be smooth quasiprojective over $\mathbb C$, and choose an SNC smooth projective compactification $j:U\hookrightarrow X$, boundary $D$. The logarithmic de Rham complex with Hodge filtration by degree and pole-count weight filtration constructs a functorial rational mixed Hodge structure on $H^n(U,\mathbb Q)$, independent of the compactification. Its weights are at least $n$, and
$$W_nH^n(U,\mathbb Q)=\operatorname{im}(H^n(X,\mathbb Q)\longrightarrow H^n(U,\mathbb Q)).$$

A **rational mixed Hodge structure** consists of a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space $H$
with a finite basis ([[def-linear-basis]]) together with

- a finite increasing filtration $W$ of $H$, the **weight filtration**, and
- a finite decreasing filtration $F$ of
  $H_{\mathbb C}:=H\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$, the **Hodge filtration**
  ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),

such that the following opposition condition holds on every weight-graded
piece. Here a filtration is **finite** when $W_aH=0$ for all sufficiently
negative $a$ and $W_aH=H$ for all sufficiently positive $a$, and dually
$F^aH_{\mathbb C}=H_{\mathbb C}$ for $a\ll0$ and $F^aH_{\mathbb C}=0$ for
$a\gg0$ ([[def-increasing-and-decreasing-filtration-of-an-object]]).

**Conjugation.** The $\mathbb{Q}$-linear involution $\sigma$ of
$H_{\mathbb C}$, defined on generators by
$\sigma(h\otimes z)=h\otimes\bar z$ and extended $\mathbb{Q}$-linearly,
satisfies $\sigma^2=\mathrm{id}$ and $\sigma(cz)=\bar c\,\sigma(z)$ for
$c\in\mathbb C$ ([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). It preserves the
subspace $W_aH_{\mathbb C}:=(W_aH)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb C$ for every $a$,
so it descends to each graded piece
$\operatorname{Gr}^W_aH_{\mathbb C}:=W_aH_{\mathbb C}/W_{a-1}H_{\mathbb C}$
([[def-associated-graded-object-of-a-filtered-object]]). The **conjugate
Hodge filtration** is $\bar F^q:=\sigma(F^q)$, a finite decreasing filtration
of $H_{\mathbb C}$.

**Opposition.** Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbb C$-vector space with
finite decreasing filtrations $F$ and $\bar F$, and let $n$ be an integer. The
two filtrations are **$n$-opposed** when the natural map
$$\bigoplus_{p+q=n}\bigl(F^pV\cap\bar F^qV\bigr)\longrightarrow V,\qquad (v_{p,q})_{p+q=n}\longmapsto\sum_{p+q=n}v_{p,q},$$
is an isomorphism. Applied to $V=\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$ this
condition is required for every $n$, with the *induced* filtrations: $F^p$
acts on $\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$ through the image of
$F^p\cap W_nH_{\mathbb C}$, and $\bar F^q$ through the image of
$\bar F^q\cap W_nH_{\mathbb C}$. Writing
$$H^{p,q}_n:=F^p\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}\cap \bar F^q\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C},$$
the requirement is therefore the direct sum decomposition
$$\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}_n \qquad\text{for every }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
Since $\sigma$ interchanges the induced filtrations $F^p$ and $\bar F^p$ and
preserves $W$, it maps $H^{p,q}_n$ onto $H^{q,p}_n$, so
$\overline{H^{p,q}_n}=H^{q,p}_n$. Equivalently, the opposition condition requires both
$F^pV\cap\bar F^qV=0$ whenever $p+q>n$ and
$F^pV+\bar F^{n+1-p}V=V$ for every $p$, on
$V=\operatorname{Gr}^W_nH_{\mathbb C}$. The conjunction, rather than either
condition alone, is equivalent to the displayed decomposition: the spanning
condition and the modular law give
$F^pV=F^{p+1}V+(F^pV\cap\bar F^{n-p}V)$, and the vanishing condition makes
this sum direct; descending induction through the finite filtration gives
$F^pV=\bigoplus_{a\ge p}(F^aV\cap\bar F^{n-a}V)$ and then the decomposition
of $V$. Conversely, the decomposition gives these two conditions by grouping
its summands by the first and second indices.

**Morphisms.** A morphism $f\colon H\to K$ of rational mixed Hodge structures
is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear map with $f(W_aH)\subseteq W_aK$ for all $a$ and
$f_{\mathbb C}(F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq F^pK_{\mathbb C}$ for all $p$, where
$f_{\mathbb C}=f\otimes\mathrm{id}$. Such an $f$ commutes with the
conjugations $\sigma$, hence also satisfies
$f_{\mathbb C}(\bar F^pH_{\mathbb C})\subseteq\bar F^pK_{\mathbb C}$.

**Substructures, pure structures, Tate.** A subspace $H'\subseteq H$ with the
induced filtrations $W_aH'=H'\cap W_aH$ and
$F^pH'_{\mathbb C}=H'_{\mathbb C}\cap F^pH_{\mathbb C}$ is a **substructure**
when the induced filtrations again satisfy the opposition condition on every
graded piece, and a quotient $H\to Q$ with the quotient filtrations is a
**quotient structure** under the same requirement; that the kernel, image and
cokernel of a morphism do carry such structures is not part of the definition
and is proved in the strictness lemma below. A structure is **pure of weight
$n$** when $W_{n-1}H=0$ and $W_nH=H$; the opposition condition then says that
$H_{\mathbb C}=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H^{p,q}$ with
$H^{p,q}=F^p\cap\bar F^q$, and $\overline{H^{p,q}}=H^{q,p}$. The **Tate
structure** $\mathbb Q(r)$, for $r\in\mathbb Z$, is the pure structure of
weight $-2r$ with $\mathbb Q(r)_{\mathbb C}=\mathbb C$ concentrated in type
$(-r,-r)$, that is $H^{-r,-r}=\mathbb C$ and $H^{p,q}=0$ for
$(p,q)\ne(-r,-r)$.

**Tensor and dual conventions.** The tensor product $H\otimes K$ carries
$$W_a(H\otimes K)=\sum_{b+c=a}W_bH\otimes W_cK,\qquad F^p(H\otimes K)_{\mathbb C}=\sum_{b+c=p}F^bH_{\mathbb C}\otimes F^cK_{\mathbb C},$$
where the sums of subspaces are those of the complexifications, and the dual
$H^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(H,\mathbb Q)$ carries
$$W_aH^*=\{u:u(W_{-a-1}H)=0\},\qquad F^pH^*_{\mathbb C}=\{u:u(F^{1-p}H_{\mathbb C})=0\}.$$

**Polarizability.** A pure rational Hodge structure $H$ of weight $n$ is
**polarizable** when it carries a rational bilinear form $Q$ of parity
$(-1)^n$ that pairs only complementary Hodge types, i.e.
$Q(H^{p,q},H^{p',q'})=0$ unless $p'=n-p$ and $q'=n-q$, and whose
Weil-operator Hermitian form $h(u,v):=Q(Cu,\bar v)$, where the Weil operator
$C$ acts as $i^{p-q}$ on $H^{p,q}$, is positive definite.

No mixed structure in this definition is assumed to split over $\mathbb R$ or
over $\mathbb Q$; the Deligne splitting constructed below is a decomposition
over $\mathbb C$ only.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

By [F1] and [F2], $H^0(X;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$, $H^1(X;\mathbb Q)=0$, $H^2(X;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$; $H^0(D^{[1]};\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q^2$ and $H^1(D^{[1]};\mathbb Q)=0$; and $H^0(U;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$, $H^1(U;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q$, $H^2(U;\mathbb Q)=0$, the generator being the meridian class dual to the circle.

The logarithmic generator. By the residue normalization of [F3] the class $(2\pi i)^{-1}dz/z$ is a nonzero rational class in $H^1(U;\mathbb Q)$ pairing by $1$ with the positively oriented meridian, so it generates the one-dimensional space $H^1(U;\mathbb Q)$ of step 1.1; its normalized rational residue coordinates at $0$ and $\infty$ are $1$ and $-1$, because in the coordinate $w=1/z$ at infinity the form $dz/z$ equals $-dw/w$.

The weight spectral sequence. Only $a=0,1$ contribute. The $a=0$ column has $E_1^{0,0}=\mathbb Q(0)$, $E_1^{0,1}=0$, $E_1^{0,2}=H^2(\mathbb P^1;\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q(-1)$, pure of weight $2$ and type $(1,1)$; the $a=1$ column has $E_1^{-1,2}=\mathbb Q(-1)^2$ and is otherwise zero. The sole possible nonzero differential is $d_1:E_1^{-1,2}\to E_1^{0,2}$, a pure Hodge morphism. Since the sequence degenerates at $E_2$ and $H^2(U)=0$ by step 1.1, its cokernel is zero, so its rank is one. The global closed logarithmic form of step 2.1 has normalized residue vector $(1,-1)$, which must survive this differential because it represents an actual cohomology class; hence this vector lies in its kernel. A rank-one map from a two-dimensional space has one-dimensional kernel, so $\ker d_1=\mathbb Q(1,-1)\cong\mathbb Q(-1)$. Equivalently, in a rational target generator normalized to the nonzero image of $(1,0)$, $d_1(r_0,r_\infty)=r_0+r_\infty$. Thus $E_2^{-1,2}=\mathbb Q(-1)$, $E_2^{0,2}=0$, $E_2^{0,0}=\mathbb Q(0)$, and all remaining terms vanish. This computes the required weight-graded piece without assuming an unproved Gysin normalization.

The mixed Hodge structure on $H^1(U,\mathbb Q)$. By [F3] the weight-graded piece $\operatorname{Gr}^W_mH^1(U;\mathbb Q)$ is $E_2^{1-m,m}$, so by step 3.1 it is $\mathbb Q(-1)$ for $m=2$ and vanishes for every other $m$; in particular $W_1H^1(U;\mathbb Q)=0$ and $W_2H^1(U;\mathbb Q)=H^1(U;\mathbb Q)$, which also agrees with the weights-at-least-$1$ and image formulas of [F3] and with $H^1(X;\mathbb Q)=0$ from step 1.1. By [F4] the class supported in weight $2$ with $\operatorname{Gr}^W_2=\mathbb Q(-1)$ makes $H^1(U;\mathbb Q)$ pure of weight $2$ and type $(1,1)$, so $H^1(U,\mathbb Q)=\mathbb Q(-1)$; the classical generator $(2\pi i)^{-1}dz/z$ of step 2.1 is a rational class of this structure.

Conclusion and boundaries. The weight of $H^1(U,\mathbb Q)$ is $2$, strictly larger than the cohomological degree $1$, and the only nonzero Hodge number is $h^{1,1}=1$. The space $U$ is nonempty and disconnected cases do not arise; $H^0$ and $H^2$ of $U$ are handled by step 1.1 and carry weights $0$ and at most $2$; the two residue coordinates are the two components of $D$, and the kernel computation is finite linear algebra over $\mathbb Q$; no choice beyond [A1] is used.
